front.title: DTNMA Application Data Model (ADM) YANG Syntax

author.organization: The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory

abstract.t: This document defines a concrete syntax for encoding a Delay-Tolerant Networking Management Architecture (DTNMA) Application Data Model (ADM) using the syntax and modular structure, but not the full data model, of YANG. Extensions to YANG are defined to capture the specifics needed to define DTNMA Application Management Model (AMM) objects and to use the Application Resource Identifier (ARI) data-value syntax.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The Delay-Tolerant Networking Management Architecture (DTNMA) of defines a concept for remote management in a challenged network environment, and the Application Management Model (AMM) of defines a meta-model for the structure of object types and literal-value types used in DTNMA and separates static definitions of Application Data Models (ADMs) from dynamic Operational Data Models (ODMs).

This document defines a text representation of an ADM using the types and structures of the AMM combined with the syntax and processing semantics of YANG modules , while using AMM-specific extensions for object and data modeling. With this representation, individual applications can capture their static management information in module files and make use of existing YANG processing and module-level logic (e.g., file naming, revision history, imports).

Because the YANG syntax and data modeling language are closely coupled, there is no pre-existing example of using YANG for its syntax (and its module infrastructure) while using different domain-specific language (DSL) of extensions for data modeling. Separating the syntax from the data modeling is similar in concept to making use of ASN.1 syntax of without using the SMIv2 data modeling language , which is how unrelated things like certificate profile of X.509 use ASN.1 module syntax.

One way of thinking of this is that the ADM modules use a syntax that has "YANG characteristics" but does not make use of all YANG tooling or infrastructure and do not interoperate with existing YANG modules or their contained data models.

section.name: Scope
section.t: This document defines a specific syntax for representing individual revisions of individual ADMs as text files.

It does not define a representation for the runtime objects and literal values modeled by an ADM or ODM. Encodings of values within the AMM are defined in the Application Resource Identifier (ARI) specification . While the Agent ADM provides an introspection capability to indicate which objects are present in an ODM, encodings of the runtime state of those objects are outside of the scope of this document.

It is not required that the YANG encoding be used for transmission of ADM information over the wire in the context of a network deployment. Since the AMM is designed to allow for multiple encodings, the expression of ADMs in YANG syntax is intended to support translation to other encodings without loss of information.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in .

The terms "Application Data Model", "Application Resource Identifier", "Operational Data Model", "Externally Defined Data", "Variable", "Constant", "Control", "Literal", "Macro", "Namespace", "Operator", "Report", "Report Template", "Rule", "State-Based Rule", "Table", and "Time-Based Rule" are used without modification from the definitions provided in .
The terms "Comment", "Keyword", and "Module" are used without modification from the definitions provided in .
Additional terms defined in this document are as follows.

dl.dd: The specific use of a YANG module to represent a DTNMA ADM.

section.name: ADM Module Syntax
section.t: Some aspects of this ADM module profile restrict the allowable definitions to conform with and by doing so make YANG modules defining ADMs incompatible with YANG modules intended for NETCONF, RESTCONF, or other applications. Because of this, YANG modules defining ADMs SHALL be managed separately from the "YANG Module Names" registry of . See the ADM registry defined in for registration of ADM modules. For the remainder of this document, a YANG module defining an ADM will be referred to as an "ADM module" and a YANG module for any other purpose will be referred to as an "Other Module" to differentiate it.
After explanation of extensions in , the following minimal ADM module will be expanded upon for further examples.

section.name: ADM Module Contents
section.t: An ADM module is identified, as defined in , by the module "namespace" having an "ari" scheme. Within an ADM module, this profile makes restrictions in which are formalized in the following table of allowed module substatements. This table is adapted from .
The AMM object types of are expressed in an ADM module as follows:

table.name: AMM Object Types in an ADM Module

tr.td: AMM extension statement (amm:ident, amm:const, amm:ctrl, amm:oper, amm:sbr, amm:tbr, amm:var)

section.t: In each case the argument to the statement is the name of the object instance, and in ARI syntax the object is always referenced by its AMM object type. For example, the EDD object named tx_count in is expressed as a leaf statement in the ADM module and is referenced in text form as the module-relative path ./EDD/tx_count.

The "yang-version" of all ADM modules conforming to this document SHALL be "1.1". Later versions of YANG syntax could introduce incompatible changes and will need to be examined for consistency with the ADM module use.

section.name: Inherited YANG Module Processing
section.t: The benefit of using the pre-existing YANG syntax is to take advantage of both tools that process YANG modules as well as some of the syntax and module-level semantics provided by YANG.

section.name: Direct Reuse
section.t: The following statements and behaviors of YANG are usable within an ADM with no modification:

dl.dd: The existing file naming defined in is unchanged for ADM modules. Because ADM modules occupy a separate ecosystem than Other Modules, their file stores SHALL be kept separate.

The existing concepts and syntax of modules and submodules defined in is unchanged for ADM modules. Because ADM modules occupy a separate ecosystem than Other Modules, there will not be any cross-imports between the two ecosystems. There is no harm in including an ADM module in an Other Module store, but it will have no data definitions usable with NETCONF, RESTCONF, etc.

dd.t: The existing module naming convention and recommendation from is strengthened to a requirement for ADM modules. All ADM modules SHALL be named by concatenating from the ADM namespace reference: the organization ID, a dash "-", and the model ID.

dl.dd: The existing concept and syntax of importing a module namespace, to reference objects in another module, defined in is unchanged for ADM modules. Because the import includes a specific revision, the ARI references to objects in that imported module do not need any ADM revision information.

The existing concept and syntax of the "prefix" statement defined in is unchanged for ADM modules. The only aspect of ADM modules that the prefix applies to, however, are references to feature names from "if-feature" statements.

dd.t: Although an ADM module has no use for an XML namespace (as defined in ), the "namespace" statement is used to provide an explicit ARI namespace reference (see ). For ADM modules, the "namespace" statement argument SHALL be the text-form ARI referencing the ADM itself.
For example, the ADM "example-adm" will have a namespace of ari://example/adm/ which is valid YANG but does not conform to the guidelines of .

dl.dd: The existing concept and use of the "organization" statement defined in is unchanged for ADM modules. The organization statement is augmented for ADM modules by adding an amm:enum substatement as defined in .

The existing name resolution logic described in is unchanged for ADM modules. Because ADM modules are a flat object namespace, the complexity of namespaces is significantly simplified compared to Other Modules.

The existing definition and use of features as described in is unchanged for ADM modules. This includes the declaration of a "feature" statement within an ADM module and the conditioning of the presence of an object on an "if-feature" statement. This also treats feature identifiers as module-prefix-qualified references.
The existing status, description, and reference statements are unchanged from their definitions in Sections , , and respectively.

The existing grouping and uses statements and logic described in is unchanged for ADM modules generally. Because ADM modules are a flat object namespace, the utility of reuse in an ADM module is limited to the contents of object definitions as shown in . See for author considerations about the distinction between semantic type groupings and TYPEDEF instances.

section.name: Restrictions and Exclusions
section.t: Because of the different interpretation of data definitions for an ADM module, the following restrictions are used to limit pre-existing valid YANG syntax within an ADM module:

dl.dd: Because ADM modules have data that ultimately follows the AMM value model (see ), the built-in types listed in , the "type" statement of , and the "typedef" statement of are used to express the AMM semantic types and TYPEDEF objects defined in this document. The normative mapping from AMM built-in value types to YANG types is defined in . YANG built-in types, "type", and "typedef" statements SHALL only be used within the semantic type statements () and the TYPEDEF object () as defined by this document, and SHALL NOT be used to model data directly the way Other Modules do.

As defined in this document, there is no direct deterministic mapping between the complex, hierarchical, named data nodes of YANG and unnamed AMM values. An ADM module SHALL NOT contain any YANG data node statements other than "leaf", among them "container", "leaf-list", "list", "anydata", "anyxml", and "choice". The "leaf" statement SHALL be used solely with option "config false" to represent EDD objects as defined in .

Rather than being an extrinsic notion of presence or absence, AMM objects can use type unions with the NULL type to indicate optional values and AMM values can use the null value to represent that state. In the case of formal parameters, the use of a "default" statement is used to indicate behavior when an actual parameter is undefined. In any case, the AMM value is always present when defined in the structure of an AMM object. An ADM module SHALL NOT contain any "mandatory" statements.

Because of the flat structure of an ADM, the nesting allowed and encouraged by , are not allowed to be present in an ADM module. An ADM module SHALL contain all AMM object definitions at the top (module) level.

The ADM module makes no use of XML or XPath in its definitions or logical constraints, so the behaviors described in and in statements containing XPath expressions ("must", "when", "path", "augment") do not apply to ADM modules. All references in an ADM module take the form of an ARI.

Because an ADM module will not be used for modeling in NETCONF and related protocols, the statements associated with NETCONF operations (notably "action", "notification", "rpc") SHALL NOT be present in an ADM module.

Because the transport of AMM values takes the form of an ARI, which does not include identity information the way XML elements do, the concept of extending an existing Legacy model by another model as described in cannot apply to an ADM. The model extension "augment" statement SHALL NOT be present in an ADM module.

section.name: Built-In Types, TYPEDEFs, and Semantic Types
section.t: As discussed in , the AMM value model of is expressed in an ADM module using the native YANG type system of . AMM values do not have explicit data-node identifiers and are represented as ARIs at runtime, but the static typing of those values within an ADM uses the named types of the ietf-amm module with "type" statements and "typedef" statements as defined in this document.

Each AMM built-in value type (see ) maps to a YANG type as shown in . Each AMM built-in value type is represented as a named type in the ietf-amm module and referenced by its module-qualified name (for example, UINT as amm:uint). Each named type wraps the corresponding YANG base type (for example, uint32), as shown in .

table.name: AMM Built-In Value Type to YANG Type Mapping

tr.td: string (ARI text form of any literal value)
string (text form of an ARI referencing an object)
string (text form of an ARI referencing a namespace)

section.t: The AMM built-in types mapped to named types derived from string in hold the ARI text form of the value (). When an AMM value is present in the syntax of a YANG module, it is present only as that text form, without the ari: scheme prefix but in many cases with its ARI literal type segment. For example, a REAL64 value of 3.14 is written as the untyped literal 3.14. A TP value is written as its RFC 3339 date-time or fractional-seconds text form (e.g., /TP/20230102T030405Z), and a TD value as its RFC 3339 duration or fractional-seconds text form (e.g., /TD/PT5S). The OBJPAT pattern constrains an object reference: each of the four path segments of the reference (organization, model, object type, and object ID) is independently constrained to a wildcard, a single value, or a comma-separated set of integer intervals.
The TD type represents a time delta (an offset between two time points), not an absolute point in time.

The value-class types LITERAL, OBJECT, and NAMESPACE of are classes of values, and are mapped in . For each of the DTNMA object types (IDENT, CONST, CTRL, EDD, OPER, SBR, TBR, VAR, and TYPEDEF) there is a corresponding object reference type of the same name. A value of an object reference type or of the NAMESPACE type is the text form of the ARI of the referenced object or namespace (), and is expressed as the string type. The referenced object type is intrinsic to the ARI value itself. Where an ADM author needs to constrain the referenced object type or namespace, a pattern substatement on the string type may be applied. This document does not define such patterns.

Named types, including an AMM built-in type expressed as a named type and a TYPEDEF object, are referenced within ADM modules using the module-qualified name form <prefix>:<name>, in the same manner as any other reference to an object defined in another imported module (see ). A TYPEDEF is a way for an ADM to apply a name and descriptive metadata to a specific semantic type (see ). The TYPEDEF is a top-level ADM object (see ) with the syntax in . Because they are ADM objects, TYPEDEFs can be referenced by name when necessary, as in the example below.
section.sourcecode: type adm-a:mytype;
section.t: Except for the case of a simple "type" with no restrictions or annotations, anywhere one of the semantic type statements occurs in an object definition can be considered as an "anonymous" unnamed semantic type. The behavior in those cases is identical to a TYPEDEF just without a name associated with the semantic type.

section.name: Rationale for the Native YANG Type Mapping
section.t: The AMM built-in value types are a fixed set, and each has a deterministic encoding in CBOR within ARI syntax (). Therefore, each built-in value type can be mapped to a single native YANG base type, and the static typing of AMM values within an ADM is expressed with the native YANG type system of rather than with a set of AMM-specific extension statements. Because the type arguments are module-qualified references to named types, ADM modules can be parsed and validated by standard YANG tooling as ordinary YANG modules, and the native type constraint substatements (such as range, length, and pattern) apply directly to AMM values.

Two mapping rules are used. An AMM built-in value type that has a single corresponding YANG base type is a direct typedef of that base type (for example, UINT as uint32, TEXTSTR as string, and CBOR as binary). An AMM built-in value type without a single corresponding YANG base type is derived from string and holds the ARI text form of the value.

The ARI text form is used for the types in that have no direct corresponding base type because has no base type that directly represents a 32-bit or 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point value, a DTN time point, or a DTN time delta, and the ARI text form is the representation of the value defined for ARI syntax (). Alternative native encodings were considered during the design of this mapping (for example, representing TP as an integer offset from the DTN epoch, and TD as a decimal nanosecond count or as a union of a string and a numeric type), but the ARI text form is retained so that the text form of a value within an ADM module is the same form used in ARI syntax.

Where an AMM built-in value type has a registered ARI literal type code point (), the corresponding named type in the ietf-amm module carries that code point in an amm:enum substatement (), consistent with the use of amm:enum in ADM modules to enable the compressed form of ARI.

section.name: ADM Module Extensions
section.t: In order to provide syntax necessary for AMM Object instance definitions this document defines, via the DTNMA ADM, the following extensions for ADM modules.

section.name: The amm:enum Statement
section.t: This statement is used to apply an integer enumeration to an ADM module, organization, or AMM object. Integer enumeration enables the compressed form of ARI discussed in . The argument to this statement is an integer in the YANG range 0..2^31-1 to fit within the ARI syntax. There are no substatements defined in this profile.

All well-known registered ADMs SHALL contain an amm:enum substatement within the top module statement and its organization statement. The value in the organization enumeration SHALL agree with the registration in the "Namespace Organizations" registry of .

section.name: Semantic Type Statements
section.t: The statements within this section enable the various semantic type classes, as explained in . They are all used as substatements within one of the AMM object definition statements, sometimes directly (e.g., for CONST or EDD typing) and sometimes indirectly (e.g., for parameter or operand typing), but always as a choice between the need for one of the semantic type statements. The Named Type Use (type) and Type Union (union) semantic types are expressed with the native YANG statements of , while the container and sequence semantic types (such as amm:ulist and amm:dlist) are expressed with the AMM extension statements defined in this document.

section.name: The type Statement (Named Type Use)
section.t: This statement creates a Named Type Use semantic type (see ) for its parent statement. It is the native YANG "type" statement of . The argument to this statement is a YANG type, which is a module-qualified <prefix>:<name> reference to a named type: an AMM built-in value type of the ietf-amm module (as mapped in ) or a TYPEDEF or other named type.

The substatements under this are the native YANG type substatements (see ), such as range, length, and pattern, together with the AMM type-annotation extension statements defined in this document. Because this is the native "type" statement, it does not carry the description, reference, or units statements; those are carried by the enclosing TYPEDEF object () or EDD object () when the semantic type is named, as shown in the examples below and in the annotated-uint and tx_count examples in those sections. For compatibility reasons, the arguments used for pattern statements SHALL be limited to the constructs compatible with I-Regexp of .

tr.td: Any INTEGER or FLOAT, with appropriate quantized values in the argument
For TEXTSTR as number of characters. For BYTESTR or CBOR as number of bytes.

section.t: Examples of the "type" statement are below, some as simple use and some as restriction. The constrained types are shown within a named type to indicate where the associated description, reference, and units statements are carried.

section.name: The amm:display-hint Statement
section.t: This statement provides general purpose tailoring of how AMM values are intended to be displayed. The argument to this statement is the text form of the ARI referencing an IDENT object derived from the root ari://ietf-amm/IDENT/display-hint object.

The description of any leaf IDENT derived from this root object SHALL contain specific requirements for how the display hint affects text form of any associated values, including restrictions on which built-in types the hint can be used with.

section.name: The amm:int-labels Statement
section.t: This statement provides human-friendly labels for enumerated values or bit positions within an integer type. There is no argument to this statement.

The substatements under this are either "enum" or "bit" statements from YANG, each of which define a single value or bit name within the type. A single "amm:int-labels" SHALL NOT use a mix of "enum" and "bit" substatements as this would result in ambiguous interpretation. When present, each "enum" statement SHALL contain an explicit and unique "value" substatement. When present, each "bit" statement SHALL contain an explicit and unique "position" substatement.

section.name: The amm:cddl Statement
section.t: This statement provides annotation of allowed content within a CBOR type byte string in the form of a Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL) fragment. The argument to this statement is a CDDL fragment in accordance with , escaped as necessary to conform to the YANG syntax.
There are no substatements within this statement.

section.name: The base Statement (for IDENT types)
section.t: When the type is an IDENT, this statement is the native YANG base substatement (see ) within the identity definition, which constrains the identity to be derived from a particular base identity. The argument to this statement is the module-qualified <prefix>:<name> of the required base identity. The identityref base type of is a separate YANG data type and is not part of the AMM/ADM mapping.
There are no substatements within this statement.

section.name: The amm:ulist Statement
section.t: This statement creates a Uniform List semantic type (see ) for its parent statement. There is no argument to this statement.
Examples of the "amm:ulist" statement are below, some as simple use and some as restriction.

section.name: The amm:dlist Statement
section.t: This statement creates a Diverse List semantic type (see ) for its parent statement. There is no argument to this statement.
Each of the type use substatements defines a single element within the AC, except for the amm:seq which defines a sequence of type-matching elements within the AC (rather than as a sub-AC).

tr.th: One or more of the semantic type:

section.t: Examples of the "amm:dlist" statement are below, one as simple structure and the other as a complex sequence.

section.name: The amm:umap Statement
section.t: This statement creates a Uniform Map semantic type (see ) for its parent statement. There is no argument to this statement.

When present, each of the amm:keys and amm:values substatements constrains the associated aspect of all map items to the specific type; when absent the aspect is left unconstrained. Keep in mind that AM keys are always constrained to untyped literal values and the use of amm:keys can only narrow this constraint.
Examples of the "amm:umap" statement are below, some as simple use and some as restriction.

section.name: The amm:tblt Statement
section.t: This statement creates a Table Template semantic type (see ) for its parent statement. There is no argument to this statement.
The substatements are a combination of "amm:column" statements defining table structure and "amm:key", "amm:unique", "min-elements", "max-elements" statements defining constraints on the table rows.
Examples of the "amm:tblt" statement are below.

section.name: The amm:column Statement
section.t: This statement defines the name and type of each column of a table. The argument to this statement is an identifier for the column. All columns SHALL have unique names within the same parent table.

The primary substatement under this are one of the semantic type statements which defines the type for values in this column. If present, any "if-feature" substatement within a column indicates that an Agent which does not implement the named feature(s) will: always use the undefined value in this column when producing tables associated with the parent template and/or always ignore (but not modify) given values in this column when processing these tables.

section.name: The union Statement (Type Union)
section.t: A Type Union semantic type is expressed using the native YANG "type" statement with the union type (see ).

Each member type substatement defines one of the possible choices of the union. The order of the list of choices is significant, especially when converting ARI values, because the first choice which matches or converts will be used regardless of any other choices.
Examples of the "union" statement are below, some as simple use and some with a restricted member.

An AMM type union that uses the NULL type to indicate an optional value is expressed with the corresponding amm:null member type, which wraps the empty base type and maps to NULL as defined in ; the null value denotes the absence of a value (see ).

section.name: The amm:seq Statement
section.t: This statement creates a Sequence semantic type (see ) for its parent statement. There is no argument to this statement.

This statement is distinct from the "amm:ulist" statement, which types the AC container itself, while the "amm:seq" types a portion of elements within an AC. The "amm:seq" is not present as a top-level value type except for the special case of a greedy capturing parameter type.
Examples of the "seq" statement are below.

section.name: The amm:parameter Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define one formal parameter that apply to the parent object. The argument to this statement is an identifier for the parameter. All parameters SHALL have unique names within the same parent object.

The substatements under this are one of the semantic type statements which defines the type of the parameter. When the "amm:seq" statement is used to type a formal parameter, it SHALL be the last parameter in the list and represents a greedy matching of that an all subsequent given parameters.
An example of the "parameter" statement is below, where there are three defined parameters two of which have default values.

section.name: The amm:default Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define default parameter as an AMM value. The argument to this statement is the text form of the ARI for the default value.
The default value is used in the Parameter Handling procedure (see ) to normalize given parameters into actual parameters.

section.name: The typedef Statement (TYPEDEF Object)
section.t: This statement is used to define a Semantic Type (TYPEDEF) object (see ). The argument to this statement is the name of the object instance.
The substatements under this are a choice of a top-level semantic type (see ) being named by the typedef.
Examples of the "typedef" statement are below, some as restriction and some as union.

section.name: The amm:ident Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define an Identity (IDENT) object (see ). The argument to this statement is the name of the object instance.
The substatements under this are the common object metadata, optional formal parameters, and any number of base IDENT objects from which this one is derived.
An example of a multiple-base hierarchy of IDENT objects is below.

section.name: The amm:abstract Statement
section.t: This statement causes the parent IDENT object to be explicitly marked as abstract or not, as defined in . The argument to this statement is a boolean ("true" or "false") value in accordance with . If not present, the default marking of the IDENT object is not-abstract.
There are no substatements within this statement.

section.name: The amm:base Statement
section.t: This statement causes the parent IDENT object to be derived from a referenced base object. The argument to this statement is the text form of the ARI referencing the required base object.
Similar to YANG logic, in the AMM derivation of an IDENT from a base has the following properties.

ul.li: It is irreflexive, which means that an identity is not derived from itself.
It is transitive, which means that if identity B is derived from A and C is derived from B, then C is also derived from A.

section.t: There are no substatements within this statement.

section.name: The amm:const Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define a Constant (CONST) object (see ). The argument to this statement is the name of the object instance.

The substatements under this are the common object metadata, optional formal parameters, and one of the semantic type statements that represents the produced value of the CONST. The amm:const statement SHALL contain a an amm:init-value, which is the constant represented by this object.
An example of a simple-typed CONST is below.
Another example of a semantic-typed MAC-valued CONST (see ) is below.

section.name: The amm:ctrl Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define a Control (CTRL) object (see ). The argument to this statement is the name of the object instance.

The substatements under this are the common object metadata, optional formal parameters, and an optional execution result. If the amm:result substatement is present it SHALL be used to constrain Result Storage for the execution procedure (see ). If the amm:result substatement is omitted the assumed result type SHALL be NULL with a default value of null. Regardless of the presence or type indicated by an amm:result substatement, the failure to execute any control always results in an undefined result value.
An example of a single-parameter CTRL is below.

section.name: The amm:result Statement
section.t: The result statement contains one of the semantic type statements which represents the result expected from executing a CTRL or evaluating an OPER. The argument to this statement is an identifier for the result.

section.name: The Config-False leaf Statement (EDD Object)
section.t: This statement, when combined with a "config false" substatement, is used to define an Externally Defined Data (EDD) object (see ). The argument to this statement is the name of the object instance.

The leaf statement with a "config false" substatement is the native YANG representation of the EDD object type, and there is no separate EDD marker statement. The identifier of the leaf is the name of the EDD object instance, and in ARI syntax the EDD continues to be referenced by the EDD object type, as /EDD/<name>.
The substatements under this are the common object metadata, optional formal parameters, and one of the semantic type statements that represents the produced value of the EDD.
An example of a simple-typed EDD is below.

section.name: The amm:oper Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define an Operator (OPER) object (see ). The argument to this statement is the name of the object instance.
The substatements under this are the common object metadata, optional formal parameters, an operands list, and an evaluation result.
An example of an arithmetic OPER is below.
A more complex "variadic" OPER with parameters is below. Also note the anonymous semantic type used to restrict the parameter.

section.name: The amm:operand Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define one operand that applies to the parent object. The argument to this statement is an identifier for the operand. All operands SHALL have unique names within the same parent object.

section.name: The amm:sbr Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define a State Based Rule object (see ). The argument to this statement is the name of the object instance.
The substatements under this are the common object metadata, the action to execute upon trigger, and rule control fields defined below.
An example of an SBR with some default fields is below.

section.name: The amm:min-interval Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define the Minimum Interval field of SBR objects. The argument to this statement is the text form of a TD value. If not present, the default value of zero (meaning no minimum) is used.

section.name: The amm:max-count Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define the Maximum Count field of SBR and TBR objects. The argument to this statement is the text form of a UVAST value. If not present, the default value of zero (meaning no limit) is used.

section.name: The amm:init-enabled Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define the Initial Enabled state of SBR and TBR objects. The argument to this statement is a boolean ("true" or "false") value in accordance with . If not present, the default value of true is used.

section.name: The amm:tbr Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define a Time-Based Rule (TBR) object (see ). The argument to this statement is the name of the object instance.
The substatements under this are the common object metadata, the action to execute upon trigger, and rule control fields defined below.
An example of an TBR with some default fields is below.

section.name: The amm:start Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define the Start field of TBR objects. The argument to this statement is the text form of a TIME value (see ). If not present, the default value of zero (meaning start immediately) is used.

section.name: The amm:var Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define a Variable (VAR) object (see ). The argument to this statement is the name of the object instance.

The substatements under this are the common object metadata, optional formal parameters, one of the semantic type statements that represents the stored-and-produced value of the VAR, and an optional initializer expression.
An example of a simple-typed VAR with an initializer value is below.

section.name: The amm:init-value Statement
section.t: This statement is used to define CONST values and VAR initial state as an AMM value. The argument to this statement is the text form of the ARI for the initial value.
The initializer is used as part of the Agent Initialization procedure, (see ) and when new VAR objects are defined in an ODM.

section.title: ADM Author Considerations
section.t: All of the logical design considerations from apply to authors of ADM modules when considering the naming and behaviors of AMM object instances.
All of the lifecycle considerations for YANG modules from apply to those statements reused for ADM modules as defined in . Specifically the guidance from regarding feature use and scoping.
Although this specification allows semantic type statements to be included in a grouping statement, it is RECOMMENDED that ADM authors make use of named TYPEDEF object where possible.

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: This document defines a syntax for encoding DTNMA ADMs within a text file, and for interpreting extensions to the YANG language to support modeling of AMM objects and ARI values. It does not address what the contents of those ADMs are or any security considerations associated with the data models themselves.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: [NOTE to the RFC Editor: please remove this section before publication, as well as the reference to , , and .]

This section records the status of known implementations of the protocol defined by this specification at the time of posting of this Internet-Draft, and is based on a proposal described in . The description of implementations in this section is intended to assist the IETF in its decision processes in progressing drafts to RFCs. Please note that the listing of any individual implementation here does not imply endorsement by the IETF. Furthermore, no effort has been spent to verify the information presented here that was supplied by IETF contributors. This is not intended as, and must not be construed to be, a catalog of available implementations or their features. Readers are advised to note that other implementations can exist.

A full implementation in Python language of the ADM module encoding and decoding, and for translating between ARI text name and integer enumeration (based on ADM contents) is present in the source repository . This repository includes unit test vectors for verifying ADM module encoding and decoding and is used as the basis of ADM syntax checking and formatting tools in the ADM modules in this document.
The ADM modules present in Appendix A through D are version controlled in their original form in the repository .

An implementation of the models themselves is part of the C11 language REFDA library managed under the source repository . This project has built-item (executable) testing which exercises the AMM-level interface of the REFDA through sending specific EXECSET values and observing subsequent RPTSET values as well as daemon log events.
